phonemes.desc: Voiced velar stop [ɡ] followed by a nasal cluster. In Woiwurrung orthography the 'gn' sequence may represent a palatal or velar nasal quality; many Victorian-language sources render it as a single syllable onset.
Mid back rounded vowel [o], lengthened in stressed position; the name's first syllable carries the stress.
Labial glide [w] plus close front vowel [i]; the second syllable is light and rising, like 'wee'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GNOH-wee' — stress the first syllable, keep the final vowel bright and short. Some Woiwurrung speakers render the initial cluster closer to 'NOH-wee' or 'NYOH-wee'.

kin.label: Woiwurrung
kin.form: Gnowee, the Sun Woman of the Wurundjeri people; recorded in nineteenth-century Protector accounts and later ethnographic collections.

kin.label: Kulin nations
kin.form: Related solar figures appear across the Kulin cultural bloc, each owned by the language group that tells the story.

kin.label: English
kin.form: 'Sun Woman' or 'Torch Woman' — the common gloss used in retellings for wider audiences.

pronunciation.note: The PuniCodex restoration is Gnowee, capitalizing the conventional Woiwurrung spelling. The ASCII form gnowee loses only the proper-name capitalization; it preserves all letters. Because no distinctive diacritic, length mark, or special letter is required to recover the spoken name, the entry is classified Tier 2. The Unicode form remains the scholarly citation form.

domains.title: The Sun Woman
domains.subtitle: Light, Search, and Maternal Devotion
domains.lead: Gnowee is the sun of the Wurundjeri people. In the Kulin telling she was once a woman who went up into the sky carrying a bark torch, searching for the child she had lost in the eternal darkness below. Her daily journey across the heavens is that search still in progress: when her torch burns bright, the world is day; when it dims and gutters, evening comes; when she stops to rekindle it, night falls. She is therefore light-giver, wanderer, and bereaved mother at once.

cards.name: Solar Light
cards.desc: Her torch is the sun itself; she illuminates the land so that life can continue and the search can go on.

cards.name: Maternal Search
cards.desc: The sun's daily movement is interpreted as a mother still looking for her lost son beneath the dark earth.

cards.name: Day and Night
cards.desc: Dawn, noon, dusk, and darkness are read as the changing state of her bark torch rather than as separate powers.

cards.name: Wurundjeri Cosmos
cards.desc: Her story anchors a specifically Woiwurrung understanding of sky, country, and the moral obligations carried by fire.

symbols.name: Bark torch
symbols.meaning: The sun itself; a domestic fire carried into the sky and kept alight across the day

symbols.name: Yam stick / digging stick
symbols.meaning: The tool that drew her away from her camp and set the search in motion

symbols.name: The southern sky path
symbols.meaning: Her track across the heavens, observed as the sun's daily arc

symbols.name: Darkness below
symbols.meaning: The earth that once swallowed her child and that she now lights from above

mythology.lead: The Gnowee story belongs to the Wurundjeri-willam clan of the Woiwurrung language group. It explains the origin of the sun and the reason for its daily movement: the sun is not an indifferent orb but a woman still looking for her child. The myth is ecological as well as cosmological — it binds fire, food gathering, maternal care, and the rotation of day and night into a single narrative.

myths.title: The Woman Who Became the Sun
myths.text: In the time before the sun, the world lay under an unbroken darkness. Gnowee, a woman of the Wurundjeri-willam clan country, camped with her small son, and each day went out to dig for yams with her digging stick. One day she wandered farther than she meant to, gathering food in the dark, and when she turned for home she could not find her camp — the country had closed over it like water. She searched until she was exhausted, calling for her boy, and the darkness gave nothing back. In her grief she gathered armfuls of stringybark, twisted the bark into a great torch, set it alight, and climbed with it into the sky, so that its light might fall on every part of the country at once and reveal where her child lay. That torch is the sun. The version best known beyond the community was retold by A. W. Reed from the nineteenth-century records of the Melbourne district; Wurundjeri tellers of today keep the story as their own.

myths.title: Why the Sun Moves
myths.text: Gnowee does not rest in one place, because her search is not finished. Across the day she carries the torch from one side of the sky to the other, and the light slides over the land as she goes: where the torch hangs highest, the light stands straight at noon; where it tilts, evening leans in. When the bark at last burns low and the light goes ragged, she stops — and that stillness is night, the long pause while she gathers fresh stringybark and coaxes a new flame from the old embers. Then the first grey kindling before dawn is her new torch catching, and the search resumes. The story reads the sun's whole daily round as a narrative, not a mechanism: day is the burning of the torch, dusk its guttering, night the gathering, dawn the re-lighting. Sky events that other traditions count and calculate, the Kulin telling explains with a mother's errand — light as labor, repeated without complaint, for as long as the loss lasts.

myths.title: Fire and Responsibility
myths.text: The story is also a teaching about fire and care. In the versions recorded in the Melbourne district, fire is not stolen from a deity or given by culture-heroes: it is carried, gathered, and tended by a woman, and its keeping is bound to women's work and women's knowledge. The digging stick that drew Gnowee away from camp is the same tool that feeds a family; the son left sleeping beneath the tree is the caution at the story's heart — a child unwatched is a child the dark can take. And there is grief, and the tradition does not soften it: the sky's most powerful light is explained as a bereavement still in progress, which dignifies every searching mother in the community. To tell the story is to teach several obligations at once — tend the fire, watch the children, respect the dark, and remember that those who carry light for others may be carrying loss.

myths.title: The Story in the Records
myths.text: Versions of the Gnowee narrative reached print through the records made by the nineteenth-century Protectors of Aborigines around Melbourne — men such as William Thomas, whose field notes preserved fragments of Woiwurrung language and story — and through later collectors who worked the same material into popular anthologies, most fully A. W. Reed's Aboriginal Myths, Legends and Fables (1982). That provenance needs to be stated plainly: the printed versions passed through colonial notebooks, and their spellings, details, and even their morals carry the marks of the recorder's hand. The authoritative telling today belongs to the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation, which presents the story on country as a teaching about sky, fire, and care. The contrast between the two afterlives — a museum-piece in an old anthology, a living lesson on the Yarra — is itself part of the story's meaning.

etymology.derivation: The name is a Woiwurrung-language proper noun; it does not appear to decompose transparently into a common noun in the surviving vocabulary. It is treated as a personal/theonymic name attached to the Sun Woman figure. The spelling 'Gnowee' reflects the conventions used by nineteenth-century recorders and later standardized in Aboriginal-myth reference works.

lore.syncretism: Gnowee is a specifically Wurundjeri figure and is not equated with the sun deities of other Aboriginal nations, each of which owns its own solar narratives. She has sometimes been grouped with 'Mother Sun' figures in comparative anthologies, but such comparisons must respect the local ownership of the story. In contemporary Victoria she appears in educational and reconciliation materials as a Woiwurrung cultural teaching, not as a generic Aboriginal sun goddess.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Gnowee story is one of the best-known narratives of the Wurundjeri people. It is told in Victorian schools, on Wurundjeri-led country walks, and in materials produced by the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation. The figure has also inspired Australian children's literature, public art, and environmental education, where the sun-as-torch remains a potent image of renewable light and searching care.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Gnowee invites meditation on the inseparability of love and loss. The sun rises not because it is a machine but because a mother is still looking. That reading transforms the sky from a clock into a story: every dawn is the relighting of a torch, every noon the height of a search, every dusk the guttering of a flame that will be renewed.

There is also a lesson about fire. In the myth, fire is not stolen or given; it is carried. It must be gathered, tended, and passed on. The sun is therefore the largest campfire, and the obligations that govern a small fire on country scale up to the cosmos itself. To remember Gnowee is to remember that light is labor and that care can outlast even the longest night.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Woiwurrung language was not written before colonization. The name survives in Latin transcription, most commonly spelled Gnowee. The PuniCodex restoration capitalizes the initial letter as a proper name. No additional diacritics or special letters are used, because the surviving scholarly sources do not record distinctive phonemic length or stress marks for this name.

lore.archaeology: The Gnowee narrative is preserved primarily in oral tradition and in nineteenth- and twentieth-century ethnographic records from the Melbourne region. No pre-contact written form exists; the material culture associated with the story includes bark torches, digging sticks, and the sky country itself as observed from Wurundjeri lands along the Yarra and its tributaries.
